title: Fired_from_NLP at SemEval-2024 Task 1: Towards Developing Semantic Textual Relatedness Predictor - A Transformer-based Approach
summary: Learning the degree of connection between English sentence pairs with STS-BERT.

sections.title: Start with the idea
paragraphs: Two sentences can be related without saying the same thing. A question about rainfall and a description of flooding share a topic and a causal connection, even though neither paraphrases the other. A useful representation needs to capture more than overlapping words.

sections.title: The research question
paragraphs: The paper studies continuous semantic relatedness for English sentence pairs in SemEval-2024 Task 1, Track A3.

sections.title: Approach & techniques
paragraphs: STS-BERT encodes both sentences with bert-base-uncased, uses pooled representations and cosine similarity, and trains with mean squared error. The experiments combine shared-task data with STS-B and earlier SemEval datasets. Comparisons include RoBERTa, LSTM/BiLSTM, and conventional regressors.

sections.title: Findings & evidence
paragraphs: The reported test Spearman correlation is 0.81033, placing 25th. Table 4 reports 0.749 for RoBERTa and 0.4990 for the strongest listed BiLSTM baseline. Spearman evaluates ordering agreement, not the absolute accuracy of every predicted score.

sections.title: What remains difficult
paragraphs: The authors discuss mixed dataset score scales and errors on sentence transformations. Discussion: multiplying then dividing labels does not by itself establish meaningful precision loss; a controlled ablation would be needed to support that explanation.

A reproduction should verify pair deduplication before splitting and inspect scale normalization. For practical retrieval, it should also evaluate whether highly ranked results actually answer the user’s question.

sections.title: Research directions & discussion
paragraphs: Modern retrieval designs can separate inexpensive candidate retrieval from more expensive pairwise reranking. M3-Embedding provides a useful related example of multilingual representations supporting several retrieval modes.

A proposed experiment would compare contrastive fine-tuning with the regression objective, using hard negatives that share vocabulary but express different meanings. This tests an alternative training signal; it is not a reported result of the original paper.

discussionPrompts: How should a model treat related sentences that contradict one another?
Would a retrieval metric expose errors that Spearman correlation misses?
Which hard negatives best distinguish topical overlap from useful relevance?
